title: Jaggery
points: Jaggery is still predominantly sugar — its trace minerals do not offset its sugar load.
Per spoon, jaggery and table sugar deliver comparable carbohydrate energy.
If you limit added sugars, count jaggery toward the same budget.
portionNote: A teaspoon (~5 g) contributes roughly the carbohydrate of the same amount of sugar.

title: Dried fruits & dates
points: Drying concentrates sugars — a small handful carries the carbohydrate of a much larger fresh portion.
They do contribute fiber and micronutrients, but natural sugars still count toward daily intake.
Pair with protein or fat (nuts, yogurt) to moderate absorption.
portionNote: 2–3 dates or a tablespoon of raisins is a practical serving, not a large bowl.

title: Nuts
points: Mostly unsaturated fats plus protein, fiber and micronutrients — but very calorie-dense.
Benefits shown for regular small servings, not unlimited snacking.
Skip entirely with a relevant nut allergy; seeds are not automatically safe substitutes.
portionNote: A small handful (~28–30 g) is the commonly studied serving.

title: Ghee
points: Ghee is mostly fat with a high saturated-fat share — a flavor ingredient, not a health supplement.
A teaspoon adds ~5 g fat; it should be counted within total fat intake.
Where saturated fat is a concern, unsaturated oils are the usual swap for routine cooking.
portionNote: Measure with a spoon rather than pouring freely — portions drift easily.

title: Avocado
points: Rich in unsaturated fat and fiber — a reasonable swap for saturated-fat spreads.
Still energy-dense: half a medium avocado is a meaningful calorie portion.
It supports dietary quality; no single food corrects blood-lipid markers on its own.
portionNote: About half a medium avocado (~70–100 g flesh) is a typical serving.
